blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 10 (Electromagnetism), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Explain why a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a force and how its direction is found. Obtain the expression F = BIL sin θ and write it in vector form. Hence define magnetic induction and its SI unit. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cause of the force: A straight conductor carries a steady current (out of the paper) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field (Fig. 10.2). Its own magnetic field interacts with the external field, just as two magnets act on each other. The two fields reinforce each other on one side of the conductor and cancel on the other side, so the conductor moves towards the side where the field is weaker. The force F is perpendicular to both the conductor and the field.

Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule (Fig. 10.3): first finger along the magnetic field, second finger along the current; the thumb gives the force. Equivalently, curl the fingers of the right hand from current to field through the small angle; the stretched thumb gives the force.

Magnitude: Experimentally the force is directly proportional to the current I, the length L and the field B:
F ∝ BIL, so F = kBIL
In SI units k = 1, therefore
F = BIL ... (10.1)
If the conductor makes an angle θ with B, only the component L sin θ perpendicular to B is effective (Fig. 10.4):
F = BIL sin θ ... (10.2)
Taking a vector L of magnitude equal to the length and direction along the current, the vector form is
F = I L × B ... (10.3)
The force is maximum (BIL) at θ = 90° and zero at θ = 0.

Magnetic induction: From Eq. (10.1), B = F/IL. The magnetic field strength (magnetic induction) is numerically equal to the force on a conductor 1 m long carrying 1 A, placed perpendicular to the field. It is a vector along the field. SI unit: tesla, 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: Let us now determine the magnitude of the force on a current-carrying conductor

blocks.prompt: 2 A 35 cm wire carrying 5.0 A lies in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Find (i) the force on it when it makes 50° with the field (ii) the maximum force it can experience (iii) the angle at which the force is 0.20 N. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use F = BIL sin θ; the maximum is at θ = 90°; for (iii) solve sin θ = F/BIL.

book_ref.quote: If the wire makes an angle of 40° with the direction of magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 3 Define magnetic flux and obtain ϕ_B = BA cos θ = B · A. Discuss the cases of maximum and zero flux, explain how the flux through a curved surface is found, and show why B is called magnetic flux density. Give the units of flux and flux density. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The magnetic flux through a patch of area A is the number of magnetic lines passing through this area.

Derivation: If B is the number of lines through unit area held perpendicular to the field, then for area A perpendicular to the field
B = ϕ/A ... (10.4), so ϕ = BA
If the normal to the surface makes an angle θ with B (Fig. 10.5), the component of B along the vector area is B cos θ (Fig. 10.6):
ϕ_B = BA cos θ ... (10.5)
As B and A are vectors,
ϕ_B = B · A ... (10.6)
so the flux is a scalar. A is a vector whose magnitude is the area and whose direction is along the normal to the surface; θ is the angle between B and A.

Special cases (Fig. 10.7): (a) Field along the normal: θ = 0, cos 0° = 1, flux is maximum = BA. (b) Field parallel to the plane of the area: θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0, flux is zero.

Curved surface: Divide it into many small elements, each taken as plane; find BA cos θ for each and add the contributions of all the elements.

Units and flux density: From the tesla, the unit of flux is N m A⁻¹, called the weber (Wb). By Eq. (10.4), B is the flux per unit area of a surface perpendicular to B, so it is also called magnetic flux density, unit Wb m⁻² = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (tesla).

book_ref.quote: We can represent the strength of a magnetic field B by the lines of force

blocks.prompt: 4 A rectangular loop 40 cm × 25 cm is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.90 T. Find the magnetic flux through it when the angle between B and the vector area is (i) 0° (ii) 40° (iii) 90°. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the area in m², then apply ϕ = BA cos θ for each angle.

book_ref.quote: A rectangular loop of wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 1.2 T

blocks.prompt: 5 What is magnetic flux linkage? Write its equation and explain the meaning of each symbol. Describe its importance in electrical devices and in Faraday's law, and give one everyday application of magnetism mentioned in this section. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Magnetic flux linkage is the product of the magnetic flux through a coil and the number of turns in the coil. It measures how much magnetic flux is linked with the coil due to its multiple turns.

Equation:
Magnetic flux linkage = Φ = Nϕ_B ... (10.7)
where ϕ_B = BA cos θ is the magnetic flux through a single loop of area A, and N is the total number of turns of the coil. Its unit is the weber (Wb).

Importance: Flux linkage is an important factor in understanding how coils and inductors operate in electrical circuits. It plays a crucial role in the design and operation of transformers, electric motors, generators and inductors.

In Faraday's law: The induced emf in a coil depends on the rate of change of its flux linkage, ε = -N Δϕ/Δt; a coil of N turns gives N times the emf of a single loop.

Application: An ATM or credit card has a magnetic strip containing millions of tiny magnetic domains held together by a resin binder; the machine reads the information encoded on the strip.

book_ref.quote: Magnetic flux linkage refers to the product of the magnetic flux through a coil

blocks.prompt: 6 A coil of 120 turns, each of area 0.015 m², is placed in a uniform field of 0.40 T with the normal to the coil at 30° to the field. Find (i) the flux through one turn (ii) the flux linkage (iii) the flux linkage when the coil is turned so that its normal is along the field. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ϕ_B = BA cos θ for one turn, multiply by N; for (iii) use θ = 0.

book_ref.quote: Magnetic flux linkage plays a crucial role in the design and operation of transformers

blocks.prompt: 7 Starting from the force on a current-carrying conductor, derive the force F = q v × B on a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. When is it maximum and when zero? Show that a particle entering the field at right angles moves in a circle of radius r = mv/qB. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Current due to moving charges: Let N particles, each of charge q, pass through a conductor of length L in time t. The current is
I = Q/t = Nq/t
If v is their velocity, v = v L̂, where L̂ is the unit vector along the current (direction of motion of positive charges). They cross length L in time t = L/v, so
I = Nq/t = Nqv/L ... (10.8)

Force: In a uniform field B the conductor experiences
F = I L × B ... (10.9), with L = L L̂ ... (10.10)
Substituting I and L:
F = (Nqv/L)(L L̂ × B)
F = Nqv L̂ × B ... (10.11)
As v is along L̂, v L̂ = v:
F = Nq v × B ... (10.12)
So the force on a single particle is
F = q v × B ... (10.13)
Magnitude, with θ the angle between v and B:
F = qvB sin θ ... (10.14)
It is maximum when v is perpendicular to B (θ = 90°) and zero when v is along B (θ = 0). The sign of the force depends on the sign of q: a positive and a negative charge are deflected in opposite directions (Fig. 10.10). The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule or the right hand rule.

Circular path: When v is perpendicular to B, F = qvB. This force is always perpendicular to v, so it provides the centripetal force:
qvB = mv²/r
r = mv/qB

book_ref.quote: We can calculate this force by examining the behaviour of a current-carrying conductor

blocks.prompt: 8 An electron (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Find (i) the force on it when its velocity makes 60° with the field (ii) the radius of its path when it moves at right angles to the field. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use F = qvB sin θ for the force; for the circle, the magnetic force is the centripetal force, so r = mv/eB.

book_ref.quote: An election enters into a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly

blocks.prompt: 9 What is a velocity selector? Describe its construction and working, and show that the selected speed is v = E/B. Also show how the charge to mass ratio of the particle can be found by switching off the electric field. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: A velocity selector is a device used to determine the velocity of a charged particle. Electric and magnetic forces act on the moving particle so that they balance each other only for one value of velocity.

Construction: A cylindrical tube is placed in a magnetic field B. Inside the tube is a parallel plate capacitor that creates a uniform electric field E perpendicular to B (Fig. 10.12).

Working: A particle of charge +q enters the left end with velocity v at right angles to B. The magnetic force on it acts upward (Fig. 10.11), while the electric force acts downward in the direction of E. If E and B are adjusted suitably, the two forces cancel. With no net force its velocity remains constant (Newton's first law), so it moves in a straight line and exits at the right end. Particles with other velocities are deflected and do not exit at the right end.

Selected speed: As v is perpendicular to both B and E,
Magnetic force (upward) = Bqv
Electric force (downward) = qE
For no deflection: Bqv = qE
v = E/B ... (10.15)

Charge to mass ratio: If E is switched off, only the magnetic force acts and provides the centripetal force, so the particle moves in a circle of radius r:
Bqv = mv²/r, so q/m = v/Br
Putting v = E/B:
q/m = E/B²r

book_ref.quote: A velocity selector consists of a cylindrical tube located within a magnetic field B.

blocks.prompt: 10 Charged particles pass undeflected through a velocity selector with E = 4.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and B = 0.15 T. When the electric field is switched off they move in a circle of radius 2.0 cm. Find (i) their speed (ii) their charge to mass ratio. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Balance qE = Bqv for the speed; with E off, Bqv = mv²/r gives q/m = E/B²r.

book_ref.quote: When the electric filed is turned OFF, the charged particle travels on a circular path

blocks.prompt: 11 What is motional emf? Describe the rod-and-rails experiment and derive the expression ε = -vBL for the motional emf. How is it modified when v makes an angle θ with B, and why does the current keep flowing? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The emf induced by the motion of a conductor across a magnetic field is called motional emf. It acts like a battery: if the ends are joined to form a closed circuit, a current flows.

Experiment (Fig. 10.13): A conducting rod of length L lies on two parallel metal rails a distance L apart, with a galvanometer between the ends c and d, forming the loop abcda. A uniform field B is directed into the page. With the rod at rest the galvanometer shows no current; when the rod is pulled to the right with constant velocity v, a current flows. The moving rod is a source of emf ε = Vb - Va = ΔV.

Derivation: A charge q in the rod moves with velocity v in B and experiences F = q v × B, of magnitude F = qvB sin θ. Since θ = 90°,
F = qvB ... (10.16)
By the right hand rule this force is from a to b, so charges collect at the top end b, leaving a deficiency at a. This creates an electrostatic field E from b to a, giving a force qE from b to a. In equilibrium the two forces balance:
qE = qvB, so E = vB ... (10.17)
The electric intensity is the negative of the potential gradient:
E = -ΔV/L ... (10.18)
ΔV = -LE = -(LvB)
ε = ΔV = -LvB ... (10.19)
This gives the magnitude of motional emf, vBL. If the angle between v and B is θ:
ε = -vBL sin θ ... (10.20)

Current: Positive charges flow along abcda, so the current is anticlockwise. As charge leaves the top, the electric field falls while the magnetic force is unchanged; the unbalanced magnetic force carries charges reaching a back to b, so the current continues.

book_ref.quote: Consider an experiment as shown in Fig. 10.13.

blocks.prompt: 12 A 75 cm rod moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in a uniform magnetic field of 0.35 T. Find (i) the electric field set up inside the rod and (ii) the motional emf, when it moves at right angles to the field (iii) the emf when its velocity makes 30° with the field. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: In equilibrium E = vB; the emf magnitude is vBL, and vBL sin θ at an angle θ.

book_ref.quote: The motional emf ε will be equal to the potential difference

blocks.prompt: 13 Starting from the motional emf ε = -vBL, derive the relation between induced emf and the rate of change of magnetic flux. Extend it to a coil of N loops, state Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and explain the minus sign. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Derivation: In the experiment of Fig. 10.14, let the rod move from position 1 to position 2 in a small time Δt. The distance travelled is x₂ - x₁ = Δx. As the rod moves with constant velocity,
v = Δx/Δt ... (10.21)
Putting this in Eq. (10.19):
ε = -vBL = -(Δx/Δt)BL ... (10.22)
As the rod moves through Δx, the area of the loop increases by ΔA = ΔxL, so the flux through the loop increases by Δϕ = (ΔA)B = (ΔxL)B. Hence
ε = -Δϕ/Δt ... (10.23)
If the flux through a single loop is changing, the negative of its rate of change equals the emf induced in the loop.

Coil of N loops: The emf becomes N times:
ε = -N Δϕ/Δt ... (10.24)
Although derived from motional emf, this result is true in general.

Faraday's law: The average emf induced in a conducting coil of N loops is equal to the negative of the rate at which the magnetic flux through the coil is changing with time.

Minus sign: It indicates that the direction of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change in flux.

book_ref.quote: The motional emf as well as other induced emfs can be described in terms of magnetic flux.

blocks.prompt: 14 A coil of 80 turns, each of area 0.020 m², is held perpendicular to a magnetic field. The field increases uniformly from 0.10 T to 0.50 T in 0.040 s. Find (i) the change in flux through each turn (ii) the magnitude of the average induced emf (iii) the emf if the same change took 0.080 s. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find Δϕ = (ΔB)A for one turn, then apply Faraday's law ε = NΔϕ/Δt.

book_ref.quote: This conclusion was first arrived at by Faraday

blocks.prompt: 15 State Lenz's law. Apply it to find the polarity of a coil when a bar magnet is pushed towards it and pulled away. Show that Lenz's law is a manifestation of the law of conservation of energy, using the moving rod on rails. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Background: In ε = -N ΔΦ/Δt the minus sign relates to the direction of the induced emf. Heinrich Lenz (1834) found that the polarity of an induced emf always produces an induced current that opposes the change in the magnetic field that caused it.

Lenz's law: The direction of the induced current is always such that it opposes the change that caused the current.
It applies to induced currents, so to closed loops; for an open loop we imagine it closed, find the current direction, and infer the emf direction.

Magnet and coil (Fig. 10.15): A current-carrying coil acts like a bar magnet, one face north and the other south. When the north pole of a magnet is pushed towards the coil, the near face must become a north pole to oppose the push, so the two north poles repel; by the right-hand rule the induced current is anticlockwise seen from the magnet. When the magnet is pulled away, the near face becomes a south pole, opposing the pull.

Conservation of energy (Fig. 10.16): When the rod moves to the right, the induced current flows anticlockwise. The current-carrying rod in the field feels F_m = ILB sin 90°, which by the right-hand rule is opposite to v and tends to stop the rod. To keep v constant an external force equal and opposite to F_m must be applied; it provides the energy for the induced current.
If the current were clockwise, F_m would be along v and accelerate the rod. This would induce a stronger current and a larger force, accelerating the rod more and more: ever-increasing kinetic energy from nowhere. This is against the law of conservation of energy, so Lenz's law forbids it.

blocks.prompt: 16 A 50 cm rod slides at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹ along rails, at right angles to a uniform field of 0.40 T. The induced current in the closed loop is 2.0 A. Find (i) the induced emf (ii) the magnetic force F_m on the rod (iii) the external force needed to keep the rod moving at constant velocity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ε = vBL; then F_m = ILB sin 90°, which opposes v; the external force must equal F_m in magnitude, along v.

book_ref.quote: Magnetic flux density = B = 0.25 T = 0.25 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹

steps: (ii) F_m = ILB sin 90° = 2.0 × 0.50 × 0.40 × 1 = 0.40 N, opposite to v
(iii) External force = F_m in magnitude, directed along v: 0.40 N
blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.60 V (ii) 0.40 N opposite to v (iii) 0.40 N along v

blocks.prompt: 17 Using Faraday's law ε = -N Δϕ/Δt, describe the factors on which the magnitude of the induced emf depends. Show how each factor appears in the law, and explain how an emf can be induced by changing the area of a loop in a constant field. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Faraday's law: ε = -N Δϕ/Δt (Eq. 10.24). The magnitude of the induced emf depends on:

1. Rate of change of magnetic flux: Faraday's law shows that faster changes in magnetic flux give a greater emf; ε is proportional to Δϕ/Δt. The same change of flux in a shorter time gives a larger emf.

2. Number of turns of the coil: The emf is proportional to N. A coil of N loops gives N times the emf of a single loop; more turns give a greater emf.

3. Relative speed: The speed of the coil (or conductor) through the field affects the emf. A faster speed increases the rate of change of flux and so increases the emf. For a rod, ε = vBL, so ε is proportional to v.

Changing area: The flux is ϕ = BA cos θ. If B is constant and perpendicular to the loop (θ = 0) but the area changes, Δϕ/Δt = B(ΔA/Δt) cos 0° = B(ΔA/Δt). Then
ε = N B ΔA/Δt
e.g. a loop shrinking in a field (Example 10.7) has an emf even though B does not change.

book_ref.quote: Faraday's law suggests that faster changes in magnetic flux result in greater induced emf.

blocks.prompt: 18 A coil of 20 turns lies perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.50 T. The area of each turn increases at a constant rate of 0.030 m² s⁻¹. Find the induced emf (i) for this coil (ii) for a 40-turn coil under the same conditions (iii) for the 40-turn coil if the area increases twice as fast. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ε = NB(ΔA/Δt); then see how doubling N and doubling the rate change ε.

book_ref.quote: According to Faraday's law, induced emf is also proportional to the number of turns

steps: (ii) N = 40: ε = 40 × 0.50 × 0.030 = 0.60 V (twice the turns, twice the emf)
(iii) ΔA/Δt = 0.060 m² s⁻¹: ε = 40 × 0.50 × 0.060 = 1.2 V (faster change, greater emf)

blocks.prompt: 19 What is a seismometer? Describe its construction and explain how it uses electromagnetic induction to record an earthquake. What information does it give, and how is it installed? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: A seismometer is an instrument that responds to any movement of the rocks under the ground or to vibrations caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and explosions. It detects earthquakes by using electromagnetic induction to convert ground motion into electrical signals.

Construction (Fig. 10.19): A weight is suspended by a spring from a frame attached to the ground. The weight is attached to a magnet which moves inside a coil of wire.

Working: When an earthquake occurs, the ground (and frame) moves, but the weight tends to stay stationary due to inertia. This gives relative motion between the magnet and the coil. By Faraday's law, the changing magnetic flux through the coil induces an emf, which drives an induced current. The induced current is proportional to the velocity of the ground motion.

Information: The signals are amplified and recorded, giving the amplitude, frequency and duration of the earthquake waves. Analysing them gives the earthquake's location, magnitude and depth. The two main types of seismic waves are P-waves (primary, longitudinal) and S-waves (secondary, transverse).

Installation: A seismometer is usually buried 50-1000 m under the ground in a protective case called a vault, a cylindrical steel tank about 1 m wide and 2 m deep with a concrete pad at the bottom (Fig. 10.20).

book_ref.quote: Typically, a seismometer includes a weight suspended by a spring.

blocks.prompt: 20 In a seismometer, the magnet moves relative to a coil of 400 turns and changes the flux through each turn by 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ Wb in 0.010 s. Find (i) the average induced emf (ii) the emf if a stronger tremor moves the ground twice as fast, so the same flux change takes 0.0050 s. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Apply Faraday's law ε = NΔϕ/Δt; a faster ground motion means a shorter Δt and a larger emf.

book_ref.quote: This setup works according to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction

steps: The emf (and the induced current) doubles when the ground moves twice as fast.
